payload.rationale: No current data was supplied, so this rests on background knowledge through late 2025 and structural reasoning. Observed fact (as of my knowledge): Freddie Mac PMMS 30-year averages were roughly 6.2–6.4% in autumn 2025, down from ~7% at the start of 2025, with markets anticipating further Fed easing into 2026. For the Sep 24, 2026 print to exceed 7.01%, rates would need to have risen roughly 70–80 bp from that level over the following year—plausible under an inflation resurgence, fiscal/term-premium shock, or Fed reversal, but historically a minority path when the starting trend and policy expectations pointed lower. Weekly PMMS moves are small (typically <10 bp), so the outcome is essentially determined by where rates sit in mid-September 2026, which I cannot observe. The existence of a 7.01% strike is not evidence of the current level, since these ladders span wide ranges. Too high: if rates continued easing in 2026 toward the high-5s/low-6s, 7.01% would be far out of reach and the true probability near zero. Too low: a 2026 inflation/deficit-driven bond selloff could have pushed 10-year yields well above 4.5%, putting mortgage rates near or above 7%, in which case a near-the-money strike would deserve 40–60%. I weight the lower-rate baseline more heavily but keep meaningful mass on an adverse rate path given a full year of unobserved developments.
limitations: No supplied evidence; no observation of 2026 mortgage rates, Treasury yields, or Fed policy.
Knowledge of actual conditions ends around late 2025; the intervening year is unobserved.
Threshold is near a round level where weekly noise matters if rates are close to 7%.
Resolution uses Freddie Mac's first published value; revisions ignored, but I cannot verify publication timing.
